title: Mahanama and the Pot of Ghee
hookLine: a worried man asks what happens if he dies in a traffic jam, and a pot of ghee breaks underwater
carry: a trained mind rises, like ghee from a broken pot
tomorrow: some teachers say you can practice for that moment. how?

cards: People replay last words. The last text before an accident. The last thing said before a door closed.
As if that one line holds the whole person. Some people worry about their own: what if mine is about traffic, or a grudge? So does the very last thought before death really matter?

Theravada Buddhism says yes, it matters. But inside the tradition there are two ways of weighing it, and an old sutta in which a layman named Mahanama asks the Buddha the anxious version of the question.

teach.b: The first view comes from the Theravada commentaries and Abhidhamma. The moment of the mind at death is a doorway: the last thought conditions what comes next, and an action remembered near death can weigh heavily.

So families keep the room calm, chant, and remind the dying of the good they've done. A calm, good mind helps. The strongest case for this view: if any moment counts, that one does, so don't leave it to chance.
The second view leans on the sutta.

Mahanama lives in a busy city, crowded with elephants, horses and carts. He worries: if I die in that chaos, with my mind on the traffic and not on the Buddha, where will I go? The Buddha says, don't be afraid.
A mind long trained in faith, virtue, learning, generosity and wisdom rises upward. Then he gives a picture. Break a pot of ghee in deep water.
The shards sink; the ghee rises. On this view, one rushed moment can't sink a lifetime.

Both views live in the same tradition, and they meet in the middle: the last thought tends to be the one you've practiced. Max Müller's Dhammapada begins: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought."

how: In Theravada communities, families and monks often chant near the dying, keep the room calm, and remind the person of their good deeds, hoping for a peaceful, wholesome last state of mind.

o: the mind at the moment of death, which can shape what follows
the final words a person writes down in a will
a thought you must keep secret until the day you die

games.q: two ways of weighing it — tap the pairs.
p: the last moment is a doorway
feared dying in the city's chaos
rises when the pot breaks underwater

s: in the sutta, the Buddha tells Mahanama his worry is right and he should fear
he says don't be afraid: a mind trained in faith, virtue, learning, generosity and wisdom rises, like ghee.
Theravada families often remind the dying of the good they've done
a calm, good mind at death is held to help, so the room is kept calm.
in Buddhism, only the very last thought counts; the rest of life doesn't matter
even the doorway view treats the last thought as shaped by a lifetime; the sutta says the trained mind rises.

games.q: your uncle says he'll live however he likes and just think something holy at the very end. your cousin, who leans to view one, asks for its best case. what is it?
o: the last moment is a doorway, so train now the mind that shows up then.
the last thought is the only thing that matters, so he's got it right.
nothing at the end matters, so he can skip thinking about it.
games.why: view one takes the last moment seriously, which is exactly why it doesn't leave it to chance. and view two, the ghee, says the same from the other side: what you practice is what rises.

practice: Count three good things from today, even small ones: a warm drink, a text from a friend, a minute of sun. Give each one a full breath.
Then pick the best of the three and rest on it for the rest of the sit, so the last thought of this practice is a good one.

wordCard.voice: The last thought: the mind at the moment of death. One view says it's a doorway; another says a lifetime rises like ghee. Both say train the mind now.

orig.note: Pali cuti-citta: death-consciousness, the last moment of mind in a life (Abhidhamma).

carryVoice: One to keep: a trained mind rises, like ghee from a broken pot. The good thoughts you practice now are the ones nearby at the end. Twenty-three days in.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 55.21, Mahanama Sutta (fear of dying in the crowded city; the trained mind rises; the pot of ghee or oil broken in deep water)
Theravada Abhidhamma and commentaries (death-proximate kamma; the death-consciousness, cuti-citta)

sources.q: All that we are is the result of what we have thought
